text: Which of our services are still running Node 14, which is past end of life? At ten services, someone could answer that from memory. At four hundred services spread across thirty teams, nobody can, and a manual audit that tries will be stale again within a month as services ship and get bumped.

This is the same category of problem the catalog solved for ownership back in Lesson 5, except now the question isn't what exists, it's how healthy is what exists, across the whole organization, right now. Backstage's answer is the Tech Insights plugin, built in layers directly on top of that catalog.

Fact retrievers collect one concrete piece of data per entity -- the Node.js version pinned in a package.json, whether a security scan workflow exists, whether an on-call owner is declared. Checks evaluate that fact against a threshold and produce a plain pass or fail, like runtime is not end-of-life, or declares an on-call owner. Run across the whole catalog, those checks become a scorecard: a grid where every row is a service, every column is a check, and every cell is a pass or fail.

That grid makes three things answerable that weren't before. Migration tracking becomes a literal count of red cells in one column, trackable week over week. Compliance -- does every production service have scanning enabled -- becomes one check run everywhere at once instead of a security team emailing thirty team leads. And golden-path adherence, whether a service was actually scaffolded through the vetted template from Lesson 5, becomes measurable instead of aspirational.

None of it works without accurate data underneath. A fact retriever only produces a correct result if it's reading real entity data -- the repo the catalog entry actually points at, an owner field that's genuinely filled in. Wrong metadata in means a wrong check result out, scorecard or not.

That's the thread running through this whole chapter: the catalog is the foundation, the portal surfaces it, self-service provisioning keeps it growing accurately, and scorecards turn all of that into org-wide visibility no team-by-team audit could produce. Next, Chapter 3 moves from the portal to GitOps itself, starting with declarative state in Git as the single source of truth.
